title: Lost track of direction
author: FruitDesperate2705
selftext:
I’ve been trying to build websites, projects, and games with AI, but I honestly feel lost and don’t know what I should learn or do first.

My biggest problems are project management and prompting. Sometimes I ask AI to change one thing and it ends up removing or breaking existing features. I also don’t really know how to properly structure a project or manage AI context.

I’m currently using VS Code and I can switch to Claude/chatgpt app but I’m overwhelmed by all the different tools, agents, MCPs and etc. 

For those experienced with AI-assisted development:

\- What should I learn first?

\- How do you plan/manage bigger AI-assisted projects?

\- How do you stop AI from breaking existing work?

\- What tools/workflow do you recommend?

  Any good books, courses, GitHub repos, YouTube        channels, or websites?

I want to actually understand development instead of just blindly prompting AI until something works.

Any advice would be really appreciated. 🙏

comments.author: OnHappyDaymare
comments.body:
Usually, this happens because the instructions aren't specific enough. Often, vague instructions stem from not having a clear idea of ​​what you actually want to achieve. Since AI isn't omnipotent, the right approach is to discuss the task first, create a detailed document, and then have the AI ​​work based on that—making sure to update the document whenever changes are made.

And one crucial point: use a high-quality, powerful model.

comments.author: zylim42
comments.body: hi friend it does seem overwhelming because the possibilities are endless and you want to make sure you go down the correct road. But having just built my first game, i'd say just start anywhere. create a concept, even if its a thin one, and iterate on it. the final product will be nothing like the first draft but thats ok. dont worry about which skill to download, which thing to use. just start in VS since yr already there, connect to your repo / vercel and bring your first idea to life.

replies.author: Interesting-Act-1958
replies.body:
Absolutely agree with this mate! If you want a general "try reading up on x" response, I would suggest reading up on Software Development Life Cycle models.
I've found that understanding how applications operate in terms of "method 1 calls method 2" (in Object Oriented languages for example) has helped me get my head around describing the objective to the AI model more effectively.

replies.author: FruitDesperate2705
replies.body: I'll try my best. Thanks mann🙏

comments.author: Bluetails_Buizel
comments.body:
Haiku and free chatgpt has the worst experience in my opinion, they frequently break stuff. Sonnet 4.5 Low / 5 Low is good enough for my workflow. Although non coders can use higher thinking levels or better models that Claude offers.

I always save both copy’s of my code, both the old one and the new one 

Especially whenever I want it to add in new stuff

Basically, if stuff does break, I :

Locate which functions / parts of the project it frequently break

Tell the ai to plan first before writing code. He will tell you what the ai is going to add in and you can see for yourself if your idea matches his idea.

Always ask part of the code that you don’t understand, get it to explain it for you, (he cannot be mad against stupid questions.) sometimes having the human (You) to understand what you are doing is part of the process. Don’t let the ai do things fully autonomously.

replies.author: FruitDesperate2705
replies.body: I'll take note of that. Truely appreciated 🙏

comments.author: Charming_You_25
comments.body:
Use fable for planning. Read the plans and ask questions. Use gpt high to implement, medium to review. Fable to review if it seems like it’s thrashing.

Slow down, learn everything. Don’t do anything by hand unless the AI can’t do it good enough. Yes it’s overwhelming and not always fun. You’ll still move way, way faster.

replies.author: FruitDesperate2705
replies.body: I'll try switching it to fable and slow my progress down. Thanks Mann

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
Ok, for a start, this stuff is all hard, even with AI. You still need to understand what the AI is doing at some level so you can remain the last approval in the chain. It can all be learned but it is a lot to take in at once.

Work with the AI to build out your workflow:

\- Scrum will give you an idea of how projects can work. Scrum is a framework for delivering complex projects (https://www.scrum.org/resource-center). You don’t need it all but understand why it exists and adopt what you want  
\- Concepts like Double Diamond design process can give you an outline of the flow  
\- Create a ticket system (I use backlog.md but there are many) and learn what a proper ticket contains. These give you traceability and consistency between agents. A chat is not a reliable record  
\- Create a game design document with a clear top level goal of the project  
\- Create rules about who gets to approve a ticket for implementation, how the ticket is worked on and who can approve the outcome.  
\- Learn the basics of GitHub for version control and get the AI to manage this for you  
\- Learn the basics of testing (playwright and vitest in my case) and get the AI to manage it for you  
\- Learn the basics of how your AI tool is designed to work. Sub agents, context management, permissions etc to give your AI full scope to support you

When you are working:

\- Have one agent as your orchestrator that will never create code but only manages the project, helps you select targets from the backlog and answers your questions  
\- Create a new agent for each task so your context stays small and on topic  
\- Read what is produced. If you don’t understand something just ask. Don’t let the AI run away with your project  
\- You are the ultimate proof something works. Don’t accept the AI saying it works  
\- Be prepared to change direction, undo bad decisions or even abandon whole ideas. This is a journey

I hope that gives you some ideas. Game development is hard. Using AIs well is hard. Doing them both together is a fun challenge.

replies.author: FruitDesperate2705
replies.body: Thanks so much for the advice 😭

replies.author: FruitDesperate2705
replies.body: To learn about sub agents and context management, i just have to go through the codex/claude documentation ?

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
Yes, or ask your agent to use the official documentation to give you an overview. These tools are quite good at understanding themselves and what they should be doing.

It's always a case of the better you can describe your challenges and requirements, and the more clearly you can point the agent towards your acceptable sources, the better the result you will get.

comments.author: IcyBother8850
comments.body:
1. Start by asking the AI to create the system design for the feature you are about to implement  
2, Tell him to expand each point from the system design doc into actionable tasks and write them down.  
3. Start implementing the tasks one by one with AI and also tell him to document what it does.

P.S. Don't be afraid of huge readme and todo files where it documents the progress that's what will help it get proper context so it doesnt do double work or destroy previous work.

replies.author: FruitDesperate2705
replies.body: Basically the todo files include all the features ?

replies.author: IcyBother8850
replies.body: Yep, you let him create full documentation, AI loves documentation, I have main readme file that serves like an index with references/links to other readmes that talk about different topics, one is game design, another is stages of development, thrid is cross-stage contexts, forth is Architectural decision records....in other words AI loves documentation so make him document everything then he will use it to better prompt itself ;)

comments.author: DonkeyFar5962
comments.body: Honestly, I think it’s mostly about building something, breaking it, fixing it, iterating, and trying again. You learn something from every mistake along the way. That’s part of what makes building games with AI so fun.

replies.author: DonkeyFar5962
replies.body: A simple workflow that helps me is to make one small change at a time, test it, and commit it with Git when it works. Before asking for another change, I make sure the AI understands what’s already working and what it shouldn’t touch. That way, if something breaks, it’s much easier to find the problem and go back.
